description: Terbium is a silvery-white rare earth metal and the ninth member of the lanthanide series with atomic number 65. It is malleable, ductile, and fairly electropositive, reacting with water to evolve hydrogen gas. Terbium is never found in nature as a free element but is contained in many minerals including cerite, gadolinite, monazite, xenotime and euxenite.
uses: Terbium is used to dope calcium fluoride, calcium tungstate and strontium molybdate in solid-state devices, and as a crystal stabilizer of fuel cells that operate at elevated temperatures. As a component of Terfenol-D, terbium is used in actuators, naval sonar systems and sensors. Most of the world's terbium supply is used in green phosphors, with terbium oxide used in fluorescent lamps and television and monitor cathode-ray tubes, and terbium green phosphors combined with europium phosphors to provide trichromatic white lighting technology.
characteristics: Terbium is silvery-white, malleable, ductile and soft enough to be cut with a knife, with relatively high stability in air compared to more reactive lanthanides. The terbium(III) cation is brilliantly fluorescent in a bright lemon-yellow color, and it has a simple ferromagnetic ordering below 219 K that transforms into a helical antiferromagnetic state above that temperature. Terbium readily oxidizes in the presence of most acids, halogens, and water.
